## 2026-09-20 — filed through the inbox spool

### The download manifest signs the raw URL string while the transport requests its normalized form

* **ID:** f-20260920-09 · **Status:** open · **Area:** native-fs · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src-tauri/src/fs.rs:277` (the signed payload covers the URL as written in the manifest) and `:468` (the request is issued with `reqwest::Url::as_str()`).
* **Defect (reported by a lens, confirm first):** the signature is computed over the manifest's raw URL text, but the bytes actually fetched come from `reqwest::Url::as_str()`, which normalizes — a default port is dropped, the path and escaping are canonicalized. Signature verification therefore proves a string that is not necessarily the string contacted. `https://host:443/path` and `https://host/path` sign differently and fetch identically.
* **Why it matters:** the digest still gates installation, so this is not a path to installing unsigned content; what is lost is the manifest's claim about *which origin was contacted*. `docs/signed-download-manifests.md` presents the signed URL as part of the guarantee, and it is weaker than it reads.
* **Fix shape:** sign the normalized form, or request the exact signed string — one of the two, decided once and stated in `docs/signed-download-manifests.md`, plus a test that signs `https://host:443/…` and asserts the request URL matches the signed bytes.
* **Found by:** Claude Code, 2026-09-20, `$push` review of `563790ff..HEAD` (review-tauri-security, should-fix, confidence 96). Pre-existing, origin `c8fd767d`.

## 2026-09-20 — filed through the inbox spool

### The credential registry writes through a retained descriptor but reopens by pathname at startup

* **ID:** f-20260920-10 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** oauth-credentials · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src-tauri/src/credentials.rs:216` (registry writes through a retained directory descriptor), `:284-311` (startup reopens the current pathname).
* **Defect (reported by a lens, confirm first):** the two halves disagree about what identifies the credential directory. Renaming it while the app runs leaves the writer journaling into the detached inode, while the keyring token survives; the next startup opens the replacement pathname, finds an empty registry, and can neither reconcile the live token nor remove the orphaned credential.
* **Why it matters:** the orphan is a bearer credential the application no longer knows it holds, so nothing will ever revoke or clean it up; the user sees a signed-out app with a live token still in the keyring. Same identity-versus-pathname class as `f-20260918-02` and `f-20260920-*` on the download installer, in the credential store rather than the filesystem.
* **Fix shape:** make startup resolve the registry through the same authority descriptor the writer holds, or detect the mismatch and reconcile the keyring against it explicitly, plus a test that renames the directory between a write and a restart.
* **Found by:** Claude Code, 2026-09-20, `$push` review of `563790ff..HEAD` (review-tauri-security, should-fix, confidence 96). Pre-existing, origin `aba6ab7fe`.
* **Handled as a duplicate of `f-20260912-01` (2026-09-27, drain session 62f4e00e-4f04-4250-974c-cf879f3e3768):** the same defect — a credential directory renamed while the app runs leaves the writer journalling into the detached inode while the keyring token survives. Fixed by `68a70cfd` and `205264ba` through the second fix shape named here ("detect the mismatch and reconcile the keyring against it explicitly"): the keyring write is bracketed by an identity check against the startup pathname, and a detected detachment deletes the secret or leaves a verified `PendingDelete` tombstone at the startup location. The first fix shape (startup resolves through the writer's descriptor) was rejected because a fresh process has no descriptor to resolve through; the pathname is what startup uses. The requested rename-between-write-and-restart test exists as `retained_credential_directory_descriptor_is_used_after_rename` (now the refusal anchor) plus the tombstone restart tests. Decision `d-20260927-25`.

### Saving an engine's raw JSON re-reads its image, because the parsed handle is a new object with the same id

* **ID:** f-20260920-12 · **Status:** open · **Area:** frontend-ui · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/components/common/LocalImage.tsx:11-28` (the `useEffect` dependency list `[image, key]`, with `key = image.id.id` at `:9`), `src/components/engines/EnginesPage.tsx:694` (`setEngine` → `replaceEngineById`) and `:735-742` (`JSONModal`'s `parsePersistedEngineJson(value)`).
* **Defect:** the effect that reads an engine portrait depends on the `image` **object**, although the author already computed its identity as `key = image.id.id` and put that in the list too. `JSONModal` parses the edited text with `parsePersistedEngineJson` and hands the result to `setEngine`, which replaces the engine in `enginesAtom`; the parsed `imageHandle` is therefore a structurally identical but referentially new object. `LocalImage` re-runs `readEngineImage` for an image it already has, up to `MAX_ENGINE_IMAGE_BYTES` (10 MiB, `src-tauri/src/main.rs:110`) over an IPC transport that carries `Vec<u8>` as a JSON `number[]`. Not observed for an engine *toggle*: `EngineSelection.tsx:78-80` spreads the engine (`{ ...e, loaded: !e.loaded }`) and preserves `imageHandle` by reference, and eight review lenses measured that during `f-20260906-09`'s plan review — the JSON modal is the one path that does mint a new handle.

* **Handled 2026-09-20 — the leak was Vitest's mock queue, not the DOM query or a React root.**
  `BareModuleMocker.resolveMocks` (vitest 4.1.0,
  `vitest/dist/chunks/startVitestModuleRunner.C3ZR-4J3.js:103`) resolves every queued mock action
  through one `Promise.all` and applies `unmockPath`/`mockPath` in **resolution** order, not queue
  order. The file queued two actions for `mantine-flagpack` before each case's first import: the
  `vi.doUnmock` in `afterEach`, then the case's own `vi.doMock`/`vi.doUnmock` from
  `importFideInfo`. Under load they landed backwards often enough to redden CI — the rejection
  case then rendered a real flag, and a later case waited out its timeout on a flag pack that was
  still mocked. Measured directly, not inferred: a probe looping 50x
  `{ vi.resetModules(); vi.doUnmock("mantine-flagpack"); vi.doMock("mantine-flagpack", throwing);
  await import("mantine-flagpack") }` reported `{"mockWon":49,"unmockWon":1}`.
  **Fix:** delete the redundant `afterEach` unmock, so exactly one action is ever queued per case
  and there is nothing to reorder. Every case already declares the registration it wants through
  `importFideInfo`. Recorded as `d-20260920-09`.
* **Also repaired, same file: the `vi.waitFor` timeout of 15_000 ms could never be reached.**
  vitest's default `testTimeout` is 5000 ms and `vite.config.ts` does not raise it, so the two
  flag assertions always died as a bare `Test timed out in 5000ms` instead of naming the count
  that was wrong — which is why the CI report showed a timeout rather than an assertion. Both now
  use `FLAG_WAIT_MS = 4_000`, below the test timeout. Measured: the slowest real
  `mantine-flagpack` import on this tree is 206 ms and every later one under 2 ms.
* **Proof, the way the gate fails, repeated.** Pre-repair, the file run 80x across 8 concurrent
  vitest processes: **11 failures**, spread over four of the six cases — `a player named
  fide-flagpack ...` 11x, `a second mounted instance ...` 4x, `a fresh mount after a rejection
  ...` 4x, `a rejected flag import ...` 3x, which matches the wider victim set this entry already
  recorded. Post-repair: **0 of 80** at 8-way concurrency and **0 of 180** at 12-way, plus the
  full frontend suite (137 files, 1254 tests) green. Ten unloaded single-file runs were green on
  the *broken* tree, so load is what exposes it — a plain loop is not a sufficient oracle here.
* **Rejected alternative, measured rather than argued:** proving the registration by eagerly

  made `a player named fide-flagpack ...` fail deterministically (3 of 3 runs), with and without
  the `afterEach` unmock. `d-20260920-09` records it so the next session does not retry it.
* **Note for any future `vi.doMock` user in this repo** — today `FideInfo.test.tsx` is the only
  one: never let a hook and a case both queue an action for the same specifier before the next
  import. The upstream ordering bug makes that pair a coin flip.

### `findings.py annotate` self-commits an entry whose decision citation does not resolve, so an unallocated id reaches HEAD

* **ID:** f-20260920-14 · **Status:** open · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/findings.py` — the `annotate` path and its post-commit ledger validation, which reports `WARNING ledger commit for … did not preserve the write in HEAD: HEAD ledger validation failed: FAIL …: unknown local decision citation <id>`. Vendored byte-exact from `~/Projekte/agent-kit/scripts/findings.py`, so the fix belongs upstream and arrives here through `kit sync`.
* **Defect:** `annotate` writes and **commits** the annotation, then validates HEAD and only *warns* when that validation fails. So a note citing a `d-` id that was never allocated lands in HEAD and in the file; the ledger is then red for every subsequent operation until a human notices the warning. Measured 2026-09-20 during the `f-20260906-09` plan review: `1a0de1f8` committed an annotation citing an id written before `record-decision` ran (the allocator issued `d-20260920-07` instead). Two further self-commits — `eed1cfe9` (`record-decision`) and `db101615` (`annotate`) — each landed and each printed the same warning, because the file was already invalid. Worse, the obvious repair is a trap: an appended bullet saying "read `<bad id>` as `<good id>`" **adds two more failures**, since the validator treats the token anywhere in the file as a citation. The only route out was to restore the entry to its last good commit and re-annotate (`b21a4ad1`, `7ef9a9d3`) — which removes content from an append-only log.
* **Why it matters:** `./scripts/findings.py check` is a member of the unconditional contract gate and runs in CI (`.github/workflows/test.yml`), so an unresolvable citation reaching HEAD reddens the gate for every agent and every push in the repository, not only for the session that wrote it. The warning is easy to miss in a long run, and the recovery destroys log content that the ledger contract says is append-only.
* **Fix shape:** validate **before** committing, not after — `annotate` and `record-decision` already build the candidate file in a temp path, so the cross-ledger check can run there and refuse, leaving the working tree and HEAD untouched and printing the unresolved citation. A non-zero exit is what the caller needs; a warning after the fact is not. Consider also making the citation scanner ignore a token inside an explicitly marked correction bullet, so the honest repair stops being a trap — but that is secondary, because pre-commit refusal removes the need for the repair. Upstream first in `~/Projekte/agent-kit/scripts/findings.py`, then `kit sync`; `pnpm findings:kit:check` proves the bytes match. Note the project rule: nothing repository-specific may be added to this file.
* **Found by:** `review-root-cause` (Codex) in the push review of the `f-20260906-09` record commits, 2026-09-20, confidence 98; the incident above is the arbiter's own, from the same run.

* **ID:** f-20260920-15 · **Status:** open · **Area:** frontend-ui · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/utils/sound.ts:57` — `player.play().catch((e) => console.error("Audio playback error:", e))`.

A user reporting "no sound on captures in the `piano` collection" cannot be matched to a log line, and a missing or corrupt bundled resource is indistinguishable from an autoplay refusal. It is also the one remaining reporter in this module that does not go through `warn` from `@/platform/native`, so it never reaches the Tauri log sink at all — `console.error` in the webview is not captured there.

Filed rather than absorbed because `f-20260906-10`'s mandate is the swallowed *port-lookup* rejection; its plan names this line under "Not part of this task" and commits to filing it, which is the boundary `build` step 4 and `push-review-policy` §4 ask a plan review to hold. ## 2026-09-20 — filed through the inbox spool

### Five `verify:app` assertions pass against the defect they name: existence, any-non-empty-body, and a bare `null` stand in for the property under test

* **ID:** f-20260920-16 · **Status:** open · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/verify-app.mjs` — the post-close process snapshot (`:227` region, `appProcesses()` and the recorded WebKit service pids), the loopback sound assertion (`:655` region, `response.status === 200 && body.length > 0`), the attachment `prepare` assertion (`:677` region, `prepareRetireImageResult.value === "null"`), the live-session image assertion (`:707` region, `existsSync(retainedImage)`), and `readLog` (`:454` region, `.catch(() => "")`).
* **Defect:** each of these asserts a proxy that the defect it guards can satisfy. (1) Teardown snapshots only the WebKit service pids observed *before* the close, so a service process spawned after the snapshot survives while every tracked pid disappears and the check stays green — the exact leak class `e5422566` and issue #723 are about. (2) The sound check accepts any non-empty 200 body, so a truncated, wrong or corrupt bundled resource passes; it proves the server answers, not that it serves *the bundled move sound*. (3) `prepare` asserts only that the call returned `null`, so a backend that does nothing and returns success passes, because the later `reconcile` supplies the state the assertion would otherwise have needed. (4) "retirement preserves image bytes for the live session" checks existence only, so bytes overwritten or corrupted during retirement pass both the live-session and the cleanup assertion. (5) `readLog` maps every read error to `""`, so a permissions or path failure on the log file is indistinguishable from an application that logged nothing, and the shutdown assertions then report a misleading cause.
* **Why it matters:** `pnpm verify:app` is the only check in this repository that observes the real product, and it is what lifecycle, IPC and process-teardown claims are cited against. An assertion that its own defect satisfies is worse than no assertion, because it is quoted as evidence. Measured indirectly on 2026-09-20: when the whole-file staged-failure matrix was built (`ba148084`), (3) and (4) could only be reddened by breaks far cruder than the property they name, which is what exposed the gap.
* **Fix shape:** (1) re-enumerate WebKit service processes after the close and fail on any that are new as well as any that survived, or assert against the process group rather than a pre-close pid list. (2) compare the served bytes against the bundled file on disk (sha256 or byte equality), not merely a non-empty 200. (3) assert the durable owner set `prepare` actually staged — read the registry's `pending_artifacts` / `image_cleanup` rather than the return value. (4) hash the retained image before retirement and compare after, instead of `existsSync`. (5) let `readLog` distinguish absent from unreadable, and surface the read error in the assertion detail. Each change needs its own staged-failure row under `push-review-policy` §2, which is the bulk of the work and the reason this is filed rather than absorbed.
* **Found by:** `review-tests` (Codex, confidence 94-98) and `review-error-handling` (Codex, confidence 98) in the push review of `f-20260906-09`, 2026-09-20. Filed rather than fixed because that mandate is the CSP-blocked engine portrait; the whole-file staged matrix was already pulled in by `push-review-policy` §2's fifth condition, and strengthening inherited assertions is a different defect class from recording their failure modes. Related: `f-20260906-09` (the run that surfaced these).

### A decoded-image failure in `LocalImage` is silent: the read succeeds, the `<img>` fails, and nothing reports it

* **ID:** f-20260920-17 · **Status:** open · **Area:** frontend-ui · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/components/common/LocalImage.tsx` — the `.then` that calls `setSrc(toDataUrl(bytes, mimeType))`, and the rendered `<Image {...props} src={src} />`. No `onError` is attached.
* **Defect:** the failure path added by `f-20260906-09` covers the *read*: a rejected `readEngineImage` clears the image and reports the normalized error through `warn`. It does not cover the *decode*. The backend admits a file on its first bytes alone (`engine_image_mime_type`, `src-tauri/src/main.rs:1618-1632`, matches the PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP magic), so a truncated or corrupt file with an intact header is read successfully, encoded successfully, and handed to `<img>`, where the browser fails to decode it. The component sets no `onError`, so `src` stays set, the element renders nothing, and no log line is written. That is the same "a blocked image is visually identical to no image" symptom `f-20260906-09` was filed for, reached by a different route — and this one survives the fix.
* **Why it matters:** an engine whose portrait file was truncated by a failed copy or a full disk shows exactly what an engine with no portrait shows, and the log says nothing either way. The user-visible outcome is indistinguishable from correct behaviour, which is what makes it worth reporting rather than merely tolerating.
* **Fix shape:** attach `onError` to the `Image` and treat it as the read failure is treated — clear `src` so the component falls back to the same empty state deliberately rather than by accident, and report once through `warn` from `@/platform/native` in the promise-safe form, carrying the normalized reason and, as in `f-20260906-09`, **not** the image id (`engineImageHandleSchema` is `z.string().min(1)`, so that field can carry persisted attacker-controlled text). Prove it in `src/components/common/LocalImage.test.tsx`, which `f-20260906-09` created: resolve a read with bytes carrying a valid PNG magic and a corrupt body, fire the element's `error` event, and assert one `warn` and a cleared `src`. Note jsdom does not decode images, so the case drives the event directly rather than relying on a real decode; the real-decode half is already covered in the product by the `naturalWidth > 0` assertion in `pnpm verify:app`.
* **Found by:** `review-error-handling` (Codex) in the push review of `f-20260906-09`, 2026-09-20, confidence 91. Filed rather than absorbed because that mandate is the CSP-blocked URL and the swallowed *read* rejection; the decode surface is a distinct failure with its own reporting decision. Take it after `f-20260906-09` lands — it owns the same component and creates the test file this needs.

`docs/coverage.md` now carries the tool-driven narrowing route, the measured fact that the numeric ratchets never redden on this defect's arrival (only on its departure after a bad refresh), and the rule: a test may read source off disk but must not `?raw`-import a file inside `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`.

Not closed by this run: `f-20260920-06`, the baseline refresh, which was the finding this one was discovered inside. It needs a CI artifact from a run containing Phase 1b, and the `coverage:baseline:frontend` deny lifted. The recurrence guard sketched in the plan's section D is named, not built, under rule 6d.

## 2026-09-20 — filed through the inbox spool

### Nothing in CI asserts that the coverage measurement still covers every production file

* **ID:** f-20260920-19 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/coverage-report.mjs:117-157` (`buildCoverageReport` already builds `productionFiles` and throws when a file has no LCOV record at all), `:221-235` (the shrink allowance), `coverage-areas.json`, `docs/coverage.md:22-46`.
* **Defect:** `f-20260920-18` is fixed but has no runnable regression anchor. Reintroducing an eager `?raw` import of a file inside the coverage include set leaves `pnpm test:coverage` green *and* `pnpm coverage:frontend:check` green, because the covered counts do not move and the shrink allowance forgives the vanished totals. The only detector is the manual `awk '/^LF:0$/{c++}' coverage/lcov.info` check recorded in the plan's acceptance criteria, which no gate runs.
* **Why it matters:** measured in all four combinations, the numeric ratchets never redden when this defect *arrives* — a broken measurement passes against the pre-existing baseline and against a baseline written from a repaired run. They redden only on its *departure*, when a repaired measurement is checked against a baseline written from a broken one. So the class that silently retired 39 % of the frontend from the coverage denominators for a day can recur with exactly the same silence.
* **Candidate fix:** a file in the measured set that is present in the LCOV but contributes zero line, function and branch records is the signature. `buildCoverageReport` already has both the production-file set and the parsed records. The check is that signature plus an allowlist of the genuinely statement-free files — today exactly `src/bindings/index.ts`, `src/platform/native.ts`, `src/state/persistError.ts` — configured beside the scope in `coverage-areas.json` so it reaches `scopeSignature` and a narrowing of the allowlist cannot itself go unnoticed.
* **Blocked on:** universal rule 6d — this is new executable checking code, and the cheap alternative is adopted and shipped: `docs/coverage.md` now states the route, the measured asymmetry and the rule that a test must not `?raw`-import a file inside `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`. Named to Felix in chat on 2026-09-20 as section D of `tasks/plans/2026-09-20-coverage-instrument-repair.md`, with the alternative beside it; he authorised the plan's implementation, and section D was explicitly not part of it. Same shape and same precondition as `f-20260920-05`. Not a product question, so no `felix-decision`.
* **Found by:** `review-tests` (blocker, confidence 99) in the `$push` review of `2cec0093..HEAD`, 2026-09-20. Verified by the orchestrator against `scripts/coverage-report.mjs` and the four measured ratchet combinations recorded in the plan's sections D and G.

## 2026-09-20 — filed through the inbox spool

### The Tauri boundary checker is a regex scanner and cannot see through JavaScript string syntax

* **ID:** f-20260920-20 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/check-tauri-command-boundary.mjs:48-90` (`TAURI_SPECIFIER`, `SPECIFIER_GAP`, `FROM_SPECIFIER`, `SIDE_EFFECT_SPECIFIER`, `CALL_SPECIFIER`, `NATIVE_EXPORT`), `scripts/check-tauri-command-boundary.test.mjs`.
* **Defect:** the checker decides the platform-facade boundary by matching regexes against raw source text. It therefore cannot distinguish code from comments or strings, and cannot evaluate a specifier that is not a single literal token. Measured, still open after the 2026-09-20 hardening: ``await import(`${"@tauri-apps/plugin-updater"}`)`` is not a violation, and neither is `await import("@tauri-apps/" + "plugin-updater")`. Both load the module. Conversely the scanner will match an import-shaped string that sits inside a comment or a string literal, which is why `f-20260920-18`'s deleted source scan had to be replaced rather than reproduced.
* **Why it matters:** this is the gate that keeps native capability behind `src/platform/`, and its completeness is asserted nowhere. The 2026-09-20 run found seven missed forms in one sitting, then two more, by enumerating syntax by hand; the enumeration has no end condition. Each round also risked the opposite failure — one intermediate revision rejected a legitimate `from /* c */ "…"` re-export on the real native facade, and another was exponential on crafted input.
* **Fix shape:** lex before matching. One pass that walks the source tracking string, template and regex-literal state, blanks comment spans while preserving offsets, and hands the masked text to the existing patterns; specifier detection then works on code only, and `SPECIFIER_GAP` collapses back to `\s*`. The same masking pass is already named as a prerequisite in `f-20260829-04` for `scripts/rust-branch-coverage.mjs`, so the two should be looked at together — this is a shared primitive, not two scanners. A parser-backed check (the repo already uses Babel scope analysis in the IPC consumer gate) is the stronger form and should be weighed against the masking pass in the plan.
* **Open question:** mask comments and hand the existing regexes code-only text, or replace the scanner with a Babel-backed check like the one `scripts/check-ipc-command-consumers.mjs` already uses for resolved facade reach? The masking pass is small and shares a primitive with `f-20260829-04`'s Rust scanner; the parser is stronger, removes the syntax enumeration entirely, and costs a dependency plus a parse of every renderer file on every push. The answer decides whether this stays one shared text primitive across two gates or becomes a second parser-backed gate.
* **Known limits to pin as tests, whichever design wins:** a concatenated specifier, an interpolated template whose contents are a literal string, and a specifier assembled at runtime. Some of these are undecidable statically; the point is that the gate states its limits rather than implying completeness.
* **Related:** `f-20260830-17` (handled) recorded that this checker has verified blind spots and that `native.ts` was exempt from every rule; this is the same class, still open in a different place. The 2026-09-20 work narrowed the `bindings/generated.ts` exemption and closed nine syntactic forms, and is recorded in `f-20260920-18`.
* **Found by:** `review-correctness`, `review-root-cause` and `review-ipc-contract` across three review rounds of `2cec0093..HEAD`, 2026-09-20. Two further claims from those rounds did **not** reproduce and are not part of this finding: a local import with a package name in a line comment reports `[]`, and a native re-export from `"./local"` with an updater specifier in a comment reports `[]`.

**Worst-case scanning cost, measured 2026-09-20 and pinned rather than fixed.** The comment-aware `SPECIFIER_GAP` introduced while hardening this checker scans comments, so a `from` followed by an unterminated line comment scans to end of input. On a source that is one enormous line, that is quadratic: `"from//".repeat(n)` measures 3.5 ms at 6 KB, 13.6 ms at 12 KB, 75.4 ms at 29 KB and 304.9 ms at 59 KB, against a flat sub-millisecond cost on the pre-hardening checker, which could not scan comments at all and so failed immediately.

Line structure removes it: the same 59 KB wrapped at 80 columns measures 1.0 ms. The real 57 KB `src/bindings/generated.ts` measures 0.42 ms, and `pnpm tauri:boundary:check` takes 0.20 s over 368 files.

Accepted for now, with `stays proportionate on a pathological single-line source` in `scripts/check-tauri-command-boundary.test.mjs` pinning both shapes under generous bounds — the test exists to catch a return to *exponential* behaviour, not to pin the quadratic constant. Reported by `review-ipc-contract` as a blocker in the final review round of `2cec0093..HEAD`; the orchestrator reproduced the numbers and judged a fourth structural change to a security gate in one session the larger risk, two earlier attempts in that session having each shipped a defect of their own (an exponential gap, and a native-facade false positive).

**This is the same design question the finding already asks.** A comment-masking pre-pass makes the cost linear and lets every gap collapse back to `\s*`, which is exactly the masking option weighed in the Open question above — so the performance case is evidence for that option, not a separate task.
<!-- ledger-meta {"command":"annotate","effect_lines":7,"effect_sha256":"22512735217c08de725d04cf3387472a1a945e03d639d9eb9699f785d059429e","input_sha256":"1d049d1185da9c50a105878f6ebfdc305604e4c06e18a41e8abb3f6383a9721e","kind":"mutation-receipt","operation":"05707eb545ba53c08794540720b2f7d779c5c2e08bac3f685f5b15314904f6f2","options":{"section":null},"request_id_sha256":null,"results":["f-20260920-20"],"target":"f-20260920-20","v":1} -->

## 2026-09-21 — filed through the inbox spool

### Writing a coverage baseline reports success after the formatter failed

* **ID:** f-20260921-01 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/coverage-report.mjs:271-285` (`writeBaseline`), `:326-329` (`main`'s write branch).
* **Defect:** `writeBaseline` runs `oxfmt` over the file it just wrote and, when that returns a non-zero status or the binary is missing, writes a warning to stderr and returns normally. `main` then prints `Wrote coverage baseline: <path>` and the process exits 0. A failure is therefore reported as a success, and the baseline is left in `JSON.stringify` formatting, which `oxfmt --check` rejects — so the next `pnpm lint:ci` is red for a reason unrelated to the change that is being made. That is the exact trap the adjacent comment says the formatting call exists to prevent; the call was added, the failure path was not.
* **Why it matters:** baseline writing is rare, deliberate and denied to agents by `.claude/settings.json`, so it runs at the moments when the operator is least able to check a warning scrolled past the success line. It is also the operation that decides what every later coverage run is measured against.
* **Candidate fix:** treat a non-zero `spawnSync` status, and a spawn error, as a failure of `writeBaseline` — throw, so `main`'s existing `catch` prints the message and sets a non-zero exit code, and do not claim the baseline was written. Alternatively keep the write but print the failure on the error path rather than as a warning beside a success line. Either way the exit status must stop being 0.
* **Found by:** `review-error-handling` (blocker, confidence 99) in round 5 of the plan review for `f-20260920-19`, 2026-09-21. It is a pre-existing defect in the same file that plan changes, not something that plan introduces; filed rather than folded in, because it is unrelated to the blank-measurement mandate (universal rule 4b, and the adoption gate in rule 12a).

## 2026-09-21 — filed through the inbox spool

### `scripts/coverage-report.mjs` has never had its failure surface proven

* **ID:** f-20260921-02 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/coverage-report.mjs` in full; consumed outside the tests by `package.json:37,40` and `.github/workflows/test.yml:157,230`.
* **Defect:** this is a gate helper whose output is read as evidence outside a test run, so `~/.claude/references/push-review-policy.md` ("A verification artefact is not trusted until each of its assertions has been seen to fail", and the inherited-artefact clause at `:215-235`) requires every failure path to be staged or argued, with the message each assertion itself printed, recorded in the artefact's own header. No such matrix exists. Its green result is therefore not usable as evidence, and anywhere it is cited the uncovered paths have to be named.
* **Enumeration already done, 2026-09-21, by two passes** — `grep -n "throw new Error\|process.exitCode\|stderr.write"` for throw-shaped failures and `grep -n "await \|spawnSync"` for rejections reaching `main().catch` at `:337`. It found **36 distinct failure paths plus one shared sink**, including four classes a single `throw` grep misses: `filesBelow`'s `readdir` rejection at the source root and below it (`:120`, `scripts/files-below.mjs:5,10`), `writeBaseline`'s `writeFile` rejection (`:272`), `spawnSync` reporting a signal kill through `signal` with `status` null (`:280-285`), and valid JSON of the wrong shape — `{}` throws a `TypeError` at `:119`, `{"sources":[]}` reaches `config.areas.map` at `:135`, `{"version":1,"areas":null}` reaches `baseline.areas[area]` at `:199`. The full table, with line numbers and how each row is reached, is in the review record named below; rebuild it from source rather than copying it, since line numbers move.
* **One row is not merely unstaged, it looks unreachable.** The area/source mismatch in the LCOV loop (`:141-145`) repeats the check the production-file loop (`:129-133`) has already made over the same `productionFiles`/`assignArea` relation, so no ordinary input reaches it. Four lenses reported this independently at confidence 98-99. Either it is dead and goes, or a reachable input exists and the matrix needs it; that has to be decided before the row can be staged or argued.
* **Related work in the same file, to be done with it:** the two mismatch checks are an identical copy of one invariant and are the second copy universal rule 11 says to extract at; their messages share one template, so an operator cannot tell which pass rejected, and the matrix needs each row's own message. And `f-20260921-01` — the baseline writer reporting success after the formatter fails — is a row of this same matrix (18a/18b/18c) and should be fixed in the same run; its repair adds an atomic temporary-file-and-rename write, which itself adds a `rename` failure row.
* **Open question:** is the LCOV-loop mismatch branch (`:141-145`) dead code to be removed, or is there a reachable input the production-file loop does not already reject? The answer decides whether the matrix has 36 rows or 35, whether the rule-11 extraction has one caller or two, and whether the repair is a deletion or a distinguishing message per call site. It cannot be settled by reading the two checks side by side — they are textually identical — only by tracing what `productionFiles` and `assignArea` admit at each point.
* **Why it matters:** two coverage ratchets and both area-floor gates are enforced by this one script, in CI and on every local push. Every one of those gates cites its exit status as evidence.
* **Found by:** the plan review for `f-20260920-19`, rounds 6-9, 2026-09-21 — `review-plan`, `review-correctness`, `review-error-handling`, `review-tests`, `review-root-cause`, `review-code-quality` and `review-minimalism`, each naming paths the previous round's list had missed. Split out of that run under rule 12a rather than folded into it: `review-plan` (confidence 98) and `review-root-cause` (confidence 94) held that adopting it there fails the adoption gate, since no obligation of the blank-measurement mandate fails without it. The complete round history is in `tasks/handoffs/2026-09-21-coverage-blank-file-guard-review.md`; **read that record before starting.**

**Corrections to the enumeration above, from rounds 9 and 10 of the `f-20260920-19` plan review.** Three of them contradict what that plan asserted, and are recorded here so the successor starts from the measured version rather than the confident one.

* **The signal-kill row is not an escape, and the premise was false.** The plan claimed `spawnSync` returning `signal` with `status: null` would evade a `status !== 0` test. Measured 2026-09-21 — `spawnSync("/bin/sh", ["-c", "kill -TERM $$"])` returns `status: null`, `signal: "SIGTERM"`, and `status !== 0` evaluates **true**. `review-correctness` reported this at confidence 100 with its own probe before the orchestrator re-measured it. A signal kill is therefore already caught; it may still deserve its own *message*, since "the formatter was killed" and "the formatter rejected the file" are different repairs, but it is not a missing branch.
* **A second row looks unreachable, beside the LCOV-loop mismatch in the Open question.** `assertAreaFloors`' missing-coverage-report branch (`:254`) cannot fire through the CLI, because `buildCoverageReport` builds `report` from `config.areas` itself (`:135`) and so always has an entry for every configured area. `review-correctness`, confidence 99. Both branches need the same decision: dead code to delete, or a reachable input nobody has found.
* **Row 23g was double-counted.** The wrong-`version` baseline throws at `:186` and is already its own row; only the `null`/wrong-type access at `:185` is distinct. Reported by `review-correctness`, `review-tests`, `review-root-cause` and `review-minimalism`, all at confidence 99.
* **Two wrong-shape rows are still missing:** `{"sources": [], "areas": null}` reaches `config.areas.map` at `:135`, and `{"version": 1, "areas": null}` reaches `baseline.areas[area]` at `:199`. The `{}` fixture covers only `config.sources` at `:119`.
* **The `f-20260921-01` repair adds a row to this matrix.** Making the baseline write atomic — temporary file, format there, rename into place — introduces a `rename` rejection with no row today, and the temporary file needs a specified cleanup on write, format and rename failure. Its tests must assert that a failed write leaves the **previous** baseline unchanged, not merely that the call throws; `review-tests` (confidence 99) noted that without that assertion, reverting the atomicity would still pass.

So the count in the entry above is an upper bound, not a settled total: two rows may be unreachable, one is a duplicate, two are missing, and one arrives with the `f-20260921-01` fix. **Rebuild the enumeration from source as the first step of that run** — the lesson of those rounds is that a matrix assembled from a previous matrix inherits its errors.
<!-- ledger-meta {"command":"annotate","effect_lines":9,"effect_sha256":"f0be8570e529a057373bd84afc727ceb9c6d3789cd73be68a59bb2d35e58873d","input_sha256":"2820fd06aaf777b6fd964df4200bd9e52a61d7e80537012049d400c79850f4cd","kind":"mutation-receipt","operation":"80abb0bda231534a33a574019ed850cb2d655080d01838dbd0157f2cf1ae1de2","options":{"section":null},"request_id_sha256":null,"results":["f-20260921-02"],"target":"f-20260921-02","v":1} -->

**Two further corrections, measured in round 11 of the `f-20260920-19` plan review, 2026-09-21.** Both contradict the enumeration above; take these over it.

* **`{"version": 1, "areas": null}` is not a distinct failure path.** The entry above listed it as reaching `baseline.areas[area]` at `:199`. It does not: the guard at `:185-186` rejects a falsy `areas` first. Measured — `assertBaseline({}, {version: 1, areas: null})` throws `Unsupported coverage baseline format`, which is the existing `:186` row. `review-correctness` reported it at confidence 100 and the orchestrator re-measured it before adopting.
* **"Unreachable" has to say *through what*.** These functions are exported and the test file calls them directly, so a branch the CLI cannot reach may still be a live contract. Measured — `assertAreaFloors({}, {areas: [{id: "a", minimumCoverage: {lines: 0, functions: 0, branches: 0}}]})` throws `Missing coverage report for area: a` today. That branch at `:254` therefore stays: deleting it turns a clear message into a `TypeError` for a real caller. `review-correctness` and `review-code-quality`, both confidence 99. The Open question above narrows to the LCOV-loop check at `:141-145` alone, and the same test applies to it — ask whether *any* caller reaches it, not only the CLI. A branch reachable only by a direct module call is not dead; the matrix records it as staged through that caller.

This is the second annotation in a row where a claim in this entry turned out to be asserted rather than measured. Rebuild the enumeration from source, run each candidate, and keep the row only if you have seen its message.

### A failing gate leaves no record of what failed, so an intermittent failure cannot be named afterwards

* **ID:** f-20260921-03 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/gate-receipt.mjs` — `runGate` at `:263-290`, which spawns the gate command with `stdio: "inherit"` and, on a non-zero status, prints only `gate failed: <gate> (exit <status>)` before returning. All seven registered gates run through it (`backend-test`, `backend-coverage`, `frontend-coverage`, `frontend-mutation`, `frontend-build`, `e2e-container`, `tauri-build`).
* **Defect:** the gate's own output exists only in whatever the caller happened to keep. A `$push` orchestrator that pipes the run through `tail` — the normal shape, because a green `cargo test --all-targets` is about 1400 lines — sees the summary line and loses every line above it, including the `failures:` block that names the test. Nothing is written to disk: `.gate-receipts/<gate>.json` is written only on success and records the tree and toolchain, not a transcript, so a red run leaves the repository in exactly the state it was in before.
* **Observed, 2026-09-21 (this run, tree `fb0b212b`):** `pnpm gate:ensure backend-test` failed with `test result: FAILED. 1364 passed; 1 failed; 1 ignored` and `error: test failed, to rerun pass --bin chessfable`. The name of the failing test is **not recoverable** — the orchestrator had piped the run through `tail -6`. Ten subsequent full runs of the identical command on the identical tree were green (1365 passed), including the gate itself, which then recorded receipt `0517ca9ec0a4`. So a real intermittent failure in the backend suite was observed once and cannot be identified, and the receipt now asserts the gate green for this tree.
* **Why it matters:** a receipt-backed gate that flakes teaches re-running instead of looking, which is the failure `f-20260917-11` records for the frontend-mutation fence test on the CI runner. Here it is worse than on CI, because CI keeps the job log and this keeps nothing: the first observation of a flake is usually also the last chance to name it, and a green receipt written minutes later makes the tree look proven. It also means every red gate in every future push is one careless pipe away from being unattributable.
* **Fix shape:** `runGate` tees the child's output to a per-gate transcript under `.gate-receipts/` (or a sibling log directory) and, on failure, prints the transcript path and the last N lines regardless of what the caller does with stdout — so the artefact survives a `tail`. Design questions the run has to settle rather than assume: whether `stdio: "inherit"` can be kept alongside a tee without changing what an interactive caller sees (a pipe changes the child's TTY detection and therefore `cargo`'s colour and progress output, which is measurable and must be measured, not asserted); whether a failed transcript is retained across runs or overwritten; whether the path is git-ignored like the rest of `.gate-receipts/`; and whether a failing run should refuse to record anything at all or record a negative receipt naming the transcript. Separately, the flake itself needs finding once it can be named — do not fold that into this entry.
* **Open question:** can a tee coexist with `stdio: "inherit"` without changing what the child writes — `cargo` and `vitest` both switch colour, progress and failure formatting on TTY detection, so a transcript captured through a pipe may not be the transcript an interactive caller saw, and the difference has to be measured on each of the seven gates rather than assumed. That choice decides the shape: a tee through a pty, a second inherited fd, or a caller-side contract that forbids piping a gate at all. It also decides whether a failing run records a negative receipt naming its transcript, or keeps recording nothing and leaves the transcript as the only artefact.
* **Related:** `f-20260917-11` (an intermittent contract-gate test, named because CI kept the log). Root `-`: the shared cause is not evidenced, since that one is a specific test's race and this one is the absence of a record.
* **Found by:** Claude Code, 2026-09-21, during the `$push` final gates of `f-20260906-11`.
* **Handled (2026-10-07, drain session aa0d130b-da2f-4502-8bdc-30c9d3cb20d4, adopted reviewed plan):** every receipt gate now keeps its child's complete output in `artifacts/gates/<run>/receipt-<gate>.log` (git-ignored; the push-gate scheduler's run directory when run as a lane, through `GATE_LOG_DIRECTORY`; newest 100 run directories retained), streamed through a pipe tee that forwards each stream to the caller unchanged. A failed gate's last own output line is `gate failed: <gate> (exit …) — transcript: <path>` after the transcript's last 8 KiB; through `pnpm gate:*` only pnpm's one `ELIFECYCLE` line follows, so the path survives `tail -2`. The scheduler likewise ends a red run with one `push gate failed: <task> — log: <path>` line per task. Interruption drains the child's shutdown output; a transcript that cannot be opened refuses the gate before it starts; a mid-run write failure fails the run closed; no negative receipt. Open questions settled by `d-20261007-06` (pipe tee — measured on all seven gates, table in `tasks/handoffs/2026-10-07-f-20260921-03-review.md`: only TTY decoration, timings, parallel ordering and a build-cache artefact differ), `d-20261007-07` (no negative receipt), `d-20261007-08` (location, inheritance, retention), `d-20261007-09` (refuse / fail closed).
* **Commits:** `42a0f3b7` (shared `scripts/gate-logs.mjs`, retention, scheduler routing and trailing failed-log lines), `212d70a8` (`runGate` transcript, drain, trailers, async `executeAction`, push-skill prose), `ae7f6d5d` (review: short log writes completed through one shared writer/capture for both runners, tail assertion, header fd cleanup), `75478943` (fd-cleanup regression test).
* **Rejected:** a pty via `script(1)`, a second inherited fd, a caller-side "never pipe a gate" contract, an overwritten `.gate-receipts/<gate>.log`, and a negative receipt — reasons in the decisions above.
* **Out of scope (MANDATE):** identifying the 2026-09-21 intermittent `backend-test` failure itself. It cannot be named from the lost output; the backend flakes already filed separately (for example `f-20261002-02`) are candidates, and its next occurrence now leaves the failing test's name in the transcript.

### Engine removal tombstones the id natively before the renderer drops it, so a start in that window still submits a dead id

* **ID:** f-20260921-04 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** engine-uci · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/components/engines/EnginesPage.tsx:676-685` (the remove confirmation), `src/components/boards/playerConfig.ts:42-48`, `src/utils/engines.ts:259-261`.
* **Defect:** the removal handler `await retireEngine(engine)` and only then filters `enginesAtom`. `retire_engine` tombstones the application id and drains its actors before it returns, and draining is bounded by `EngineDeadlines.kill_reap` (2s default, d-20260901-18), so for the whole round trip the renderer's engine list still contains an id that is already permanently dead. A game started in that window passes the liveness check added for f-20260906-15 and is refused by the supervisor with the generic operation error. The check is only as fresh as the atom it reads.
* **Fix direction:** the obvious repair — drop the engine from `enginesAtom` before issuing `retire_engine` — is not free: `d-20260913-01` serializes engine-list and player-owner updates as durable native prepare-retain → renderer persistence → native reconcile, and records that changing that ordering requires proving every prepare/storage/reconcile crash boundary first. `d-20260901-17` separately fixes "the renderer always drops `enginesAtom` after the command returns". So either that ordering is re-derived with the crash boundaries proven, or the renderer carries an explicit pending-retirement set that the liveness check consults. Filed at `build` because which of the two is right is an open design question against two recorded decisions.
* **Open question:** does the renderer drop the engine from `enginesAtom` before `retire_engine` is issued — which reverses the ordering clause of d-20260901-17 and touches the coordinator ordering d-20260913-01 guards — or does it keep that ordering and carry an explicit pending-retirement set that the liveness check consults? The first is smaller but has to prove the prepare/storage/reconcile crash boundaries d-20260913-01 names; the second adds renderer state that must itself be cleaned up on every exit path.
* **Review lens:** engine-protocol.
* **Related:** handled f-20260906-15 added the liveness check this window defeats; d-20260901-17, d-20260901-18, d-20260913-01 and d-20260921-04 all bear on it.
* **Found by:** `review-engine-protocol` leaf during the `$push` review of f-20260906-15, confidence 99; the orchestrator verified the ordering in `EnginesPage.tsx` before filing, 2026-09-21.
* **Handled (2026-10-07, drain session 489ed094-2e52-4a23-bae9-b060d1b58f2e, adopted reviewed plan):** the local-engine removal confirm clears the selection, awaits the coordinated `enginesAtom` save, then calls `retireEngine` in `finally` on every save exit, including a successful receipt, `saved: false`, `saved: true` with `synchronized: false`, and a rejected or throwing setter. A rejected setter and a retirement failure are reported through `notifyUnlessCancelled`. A resolved receipt is not notified again. Receipts that already went through `reportPersistError` (invalid record, prepare failure, `setItem` failure, reconcile failure) are not reported a second time. An untrusted sibling returns `saved: true, synchronized: false` with no error and no `reportPersistError`, and a legacy-owner conflict returns `saved: false` with `LEGACY_OWNER_CONFLICT` and also skips `reportPersistError`; both still retire and get no handler notification (`d-20261007-10`). The confirm promise never rejects, and a retirement failure does not restore the engine. `EngineSettings` is keyed by engine id. The JSON and upgrade modals keep `${engine.id}:json` and `${engine.id}:upgrade`. The prepare, `setItem`, reconcile order of one save is unchanged (`d-20260906-10`). The defect bullet above names `d-20260913-01` for that coordinator; that decision is the A2 operation matrix, and the order this change left in place is `d-20260906-10`. `d-20261007-10` supersedes only the clause of `d-20260901-17` that the renderer drops `enginesAtom` after the command returns. The `Superseded-by` trailer of `d-20260901-17` stays `-` because that trailer cannot name one clause.
* **Commits:** `b3ad5e1e` (`d-20261007-10`), `ff529215` (handler and tests), `106d2e02` (unused `saveEngines` mock), `be2118dd` (review handoff and the qualified notification sentence). Pushed `be2118dd`.
* **Rejected:** a pending-retirement set beside `enginesAtom`.
* **Proof:** vitest `EnginesPage`, removal, `BoardGame`, and `EnginesSelect` 138 passed. A staged revert of the handler failed the order tests. `pnpm test:e2e:container` 83 passed, no snapshot moves. `pnpm gates:push -- --frontend` exit 0 on `be2118dd`. Rust jobs `rust-macos-test`, `rust-windows-test`, and `rust-platform` (macos aarch64, macos x86_64, windows msvc) succeeded on run 37584986102. Local install `be2118dd`, provenance reviewed.
* **Out of scope:** `f-20260921-05` (a different legacy-identity file set) stays open. The in-flight start-IPC race named beside this finding stays out of this close.

### Legacy identity migration mints a different UUID per storage key, so a pre-id saved selection no longer names its engine

* **ID:** f-20260921-05 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** frontend-state · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/state/engineOwnerStorage.ts:314-370` (`isLegacyIdentityMigration`, `parseHydratableOwner`), `src/utils/engines.ts:98` (`id: z.string().default(() => crypto.randomUUID())`), `src/state/atoms.ts:194-200` and `480-497` (the three owner keys).
* **Defect:** `engines`, `game-player1-settings` and `game-player2-settings` are hydrated and migrated independently, and the id for a pre-id engine record is minted by the schema's `crypto.randomUUID()` default. The same legacy engine therefore receives one id under `engines` and a different one under each player key. Since f-20260906-15 the selection is validated by id, so after such a migration the saved game-player selection is silently replaced by the first remaining engine (picker) or refused (submission) rather than resolving to the engine it names. Before that validation the mismatch was invisible but equally wrong: the player config carried an id the supervisor did not know.
* **Fix direction:** migration has to reconcile identity across the three owner keys — mint ids once for the `engines` owner and resolve the player owners' legacy records against it by the fields `compareLegacyEngineFields` already compares, rather than defaulting each key independently. The coordinator in d-20260913-01 already serializes the three keys, so the ordering exists; what is missing is a shared identity map. Deriving a stable id from the legacy fields is the alternative and changes what an id means.
* **Open question:** is the pre-id identity resolved by a cross-key map built during one coordinated migration, or by making the minted id a deterministic function of the legacy engine fields? The first keeps ids opaque but needs the three keys migrated in one transaction with a crash boundary; the second makes migration order irrelevant but ties the id to fields a user can edit.
* **Review lens:** persisted-state.
* **Related:** f-20260906-15 (handled) added the id-based validation that makes this visible; d-20260913-01 owns the owner-update ordering.
* **Found by:** `review-persisted-state` leaf during the `$push` review of f-20260906-15, confidence 98; the orchestrator verified the per-key `randomUUID` default before filing, 2026-09-21.
* **Handled (2026-10-07, drain session 66775c7d-337a-4621-bb4b-64bdef85d8ad, adopted reviewed plan):** a pre-id local engine now receives one id, `legacy-engine-identity:` plus an FNV-1a 64-bit digest of `JSON.stringify([handleId, name])`, on every owner key. Records that already have an id are not re-resolved (`d-20260901-17`). The engines list keeps a one-time `legacyAssessment` claim so a later player hydration can still find that historical identity. An untrusted engines value displays the digest and does not persist the player migration. `d-20261007-11` extends `d-20260906-12`: the assessment is an identity annotation, and non-identity fields stay exact.
* **Commits:** `012f7785` (`d-20261007-11`), `7d0efb55` (shared id), `e74a9927` (named digest constants and the handle-half test), `12e6a0bc` (review handoff). Pushed `12e6a0bc`.
* **Rejected:** a cross-key identity map inside one migration transaction. The adopted answer is the digest, so migration order does not matter.
* **Proof:** vitest `src/state/engineOwnerStorage.test.ts` 51 passed. A name-only digest made the sibling test receive `sibling`. `pnpm gates:push -- --frontend` exit 0 on `12e6a0bc` (artifacts/gates/20261007T084657637Z-1989539). `rust-windows-test`, `rust-macos-test`, and `rust-platform` (macos aarch64, macos x86_64, windows msvc) succeeded on run 37597247956. Local install `12e6a0bc`, provenance reviewed.
* **Out of scope:** the untrusted engines list still makes the picker drop a saved selection. That is the filed I4 finding and was not changed here.

## 2026-09-22 — filed through the inbox spool

### 2026-09-22 — filed through the inbox spool

* **ID:** f-20260922-01 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** bindings-ipc · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src-tauri/src/main.rs` — every command that locks `state.pgn_path_authority`, roughly twenty of them, e.g. `issue_download_destination_blocking` (`:1185-1196`), `reconcile_startup_path_owners` (`:868-889`), `reconcile_engine_attachments` (`:893-925`).
* **Defect:** each of those commands maps a poisoned `Mutex` to `Error::Conflict("path authority lock was poisoned")` and an absent authority to `Error::Conflict("path authority is not initialized")`, and **no test drives either branch on any of them**. The two arms are copied by hand into every command body, so a wrong or missing mapping in one of them is invisible: the renderer would receive a differently categorised error, or a panic would propagate, and every existing gate stays green. `cargo-mutants` reports 0 backend survivors today, which means these arms are not even reached as mutable code paths worth reporting — they are simply never executed.
* **Why it matters:** `.claude/rules/async-resource-invariants.md` requires an error path and a terminal state on every asynchronous operation that reaches the process from a renderer call, and requires typed errors returned from commands and mapped at the facade. That contract is written twenty times and proven zero times. A poisoned authority mutex is exactly the state that arises after a panic inside a held guard, i.e. when the application is already damaged and the renderer's error text is the only diagnostic Felix gets.
* **Open question:** what shape does the fault-injection seam take? Driving a poisoned lock needs a deliberate panic inside a held guard, or a test-only constructor that hands out a pre-poisoned `Mutex`, or a trait seam in front of the lock. `scripts/check-rust-release-surface.mjs` refuses a public fault-injection item or import outside a `#[cfg(test)]` region (R2 of that checker, `d-20260831-07`), so the seam has to be `cfg`-gated, and `AppState` is constructed in `main.rs`'s setup closure rather than by a testable factory. Whether the answer is one gated helper on `AppState`, a `PathAuthorityHandle` newtype that owns the lock and the two mappings in one place (which would also delete twenty copies of the same four lines, universal rule 11), or per-command tests through an injected state, is a design decision spanning every one of those commands.
* **Related:** found while planning `f-20260906-16` (`tasks/plans/2026-09-22-download-destination-recovery.md`, obligation B1), whose own new command inherits the same unproven mapping; that finding deliberately does not fix this, because the repair spans every authority-locking command and needs the seam decided first. `f-20260904-05` (handled) covers cancellation tokens on the same commands, not their lock-failure mapping.
* **Found by:** `review-tests` (confidence 92) and `review-error-handling` (confidence 88) in round 2 of `f-20260906-16`'s plan review, 2026-09-22; the orchestrator confirmed the absence by reading the command bodies and the `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src-tauri/src/main.rs`.

* **Annotated 2026-09-22 (cumulative-diff review of `f-20260906-16`, commits `0eeddbb3`, `2c6779ce`; status stays open):**
  `download_destination_is_known_blocking` in `src-tauri/src/main.rs` is the **21st** hand-written
  copy of the two mappings (25 occurrences of each literal in that file today). `review-minimalism`
  reached this finding independently over that diff at confidence 96, asking for a shared authority
  accessor so the change "does not add another divergent copy". **Disposition: `Defer` into this
  finding, not a new one** — it is the same repair this entry's `Open question` already names as one
  of its three candidate shapes (the `PathAuthorityHandle` newtype that would own the lock and both
  mappings and delete the copies, universal rule 11).
  Measured while deciding: the 25 sites are **not** uniform, which is why this is a design question
  and not a mechanical extraction. Some take the guard inside a `run_accepted_blocking` closure with
  `as_mut()`, some at function top level under different binding names, at least one chains
  `as_mut().ok_or_else(…)?` without binding at all, and the new one takes `as_ref()` because its
  predicate is `&self`. A guard-returning helper would leave every caller doing `.as_mut()` again —
  reintroducing an `unwrap`/`expect` that `.claude/rules/async-resource-invariants.md` forbids on a
  renderer-driven path — so the seam has to be chosen (closure-taking helper, newtype, or injected
  state), which is exactly this finding's open question. Whoever takes it gets both halves at once:
  the seam that makes the two arms testable is the seam that removes the copies.

**Handled 2026-10-07 by drain session 1dacb397-5433-4e1d-964e-c0b7fbf1e44a (build tier, adopted plan `tasks/plans/2026-10-07-shared-path-authority.md`, review record `tasks/handoffs/2026-10-07-f-20260922-01-review.md`).** The seam is a `SharedPathAuthority` newtype in `src-tauri/src/infra/path_authority/shared.rs` (`d-20261007-26`): it owns the authority mutex privately, so a direct `.lock()` or a hand-written poison / not-initialized mapping outside that module no longer compiles. Access is closure-scoped only (`with_mut`, `with_mut_cancellable`; no guard-returning method), returns a typed `AuthorityUnavailable { Poisoned, Uninitialized }` without invoking the closure, and one `From<AuthorityUnavailable> for Error` holds the two texts, unchanged byte for byte (`d-20261007-27`). All 54 acquisitions route through it with unchanged lock spans; `engine/process.rs::with_path_authority` and `file_workspace.rs::authority` are deleted, and the five non-standard sites keep their semantics. Both literals and `Mutex<Option<…PathAuthority>>` now appear in production only in `shared.rs`.

Proof: owner unit tests on a really poisoned, an uninstalled and an installed owner (closure not invoked, closure error untouched, exact text/category/no rootFailure, cancellation while contended, poisoned `install` fails without installing); renderer payload for both failures through `reconcile_startup_path_owners` (`run_accepted_blocking`) and `create_indexes` (`BLOCKING_GATEWAY`); exact download-cleanup warnings for both stages; the engine-image source scan asserts both cleanup routes instead of a call count; the s10 scan treats `.with_mut(` as an acquisition. Six revert anchors were driven red and restored. `cargo test --all-targets` 2033 passed. `#[cfg(test)]` seams (`installed`, real `poison`, `uninstall`, `raw_for_test`) replaced seven hand-rolled poison copies.

Commits: `61b5e792` (owner and migration), `b7c87f3b` (named `PICKER_DIALOG_GRANT_TTL` for the four picker grants, test placement, review round 1), `5e55f4e8` (doc comment, round 2). Rejected: a helper on `AppState`, per-command injected-state tests, an extension trait on the raw mutex, and a guard-returning accessor (reasons in `d-20261007-26`). Not local evidence: the macOS-only body of `shutdown_engine_launch_root` could not be compiled on Linux (the source probe hit further macOS-only symbols); CI `rust-macos-test` measures it. The sibling class in `db/repository.rs` is `f-20261007-06`.

**Correction to the closing note (records review, 2026-10-07):** "All 54 acquisitions" repeats the plan's Locate census. A recount at `61b5e792^` finds 55 production acquisition sites, so the census missed one; after the migration there are more owner calls than sites because the callers of the two deleted helpers now call the owner directly. The count does not bound the claim: the inner mutex is private to `shared.rs`, so every production acquisition, whatever their number, routes through `SharedPathAuthority` by construction, and the compiler refuses any other.

## 2026-09-22 — filed through the inbox spool

### `syncDeck` keeps a card's stale full FEN, so an exact `findFen` lookup drops the card and hides its history

* **ID:** f-20260922-02 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** chess-tree · **Root:** - · **Entry:** lens · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/components/files/opening.ts:125-133` (`syncDeck`'s `existingByFen` map and
  `merged.push({ ...prev, answer: pos.answer })`), against the exact lookups at
  `src/components/panels/practice/PracticePanel.tsx:240`, `:990` and `:1064`
  (`findFen(c.fen, root)` / `findFen(log.fen, root)`, `src/utils/treeReducer.ts:50`).
* **Defect:** `syncDeck` matches an existing card to a rebuilt one by `getBoardState(fen)` — piece
  placement, side to move, castling and en passant — but then keeps `prev`, so the card retains the
  **old full FEN including the halfmove and fullmove counters**. The rebuilt tree can reach the same
  board state at a different move number (a transposition, an inserted or deleted earlier move, a
  changed start position), at which point the stored `fen` string no longer occurs anywhere in the
  tree. Every consumer looks the card up with `findFen`, which compares the FEN string exactly.
* **Why it matters:** `PracticePanel.tsx:240` treats "not found" as "this position left the
  repertoire" and filters the card out of the deck, so a card the sync deliberately preserved is
  deleted on the next render together with its scheduling state; `:1064` silently skips the
  corresponding review-log entries, so the user's history appears to shrink. The two behaviours
  agree with each other, which is why neither looks like a bug from inside the UI.
* **Candidate fix:** carry the rebuilt `pos.fen` forward instead of `prev.fen`
  (`merged.push({ ...prev, fen: pos.fen, answer: pos.answer })`), or make the consumers look up by
  board state through the same `getBoardState` comparison the merge already uses. The two must
  agree; today the write side compares board state and the read side compares the full string.
* **Found by:** `review-chess-semantics` (blocker, confidence 98) in round 1 of the plan review for
  `f-20260906-23`, 2026-09-22. Filed rather than folded in: no obligation of that finding's mandate
  fails without it (rule 12a adoption gate). The orchestrator verified both halves in source —
  `merged.push({ ...prev, answer: pos.answer })` at `opening.ts:133` and the exact `findFen`
  comparison at `treeReducer.ts:50`.

**Handled 2026-09-23 in `b912b802`, during the f-20260906-23 build.** Folded in because the same function was being changed there: `syncDeck` now carries the rebuilt `pos.fen` forward and counts a changed FEN or answer as `updated`, and `999903c0` makes the panel persist updated cards. That is the finding's first candidate fix. The read side still compares exact strings (`findFen`), which is now consistent because the write side stores the tree's current FEN. Review-log entries written under an older FEN are still looked up exactly in the logs modal; that belongs to `f-20260922-03`.

## 2026-09-22 — filed through the inbox spool

### The practice logs modal numbers every move from the wrong side and keys its cards by a repeating FEN

* **ID:** f-20260922-03 · **Status:** open · **Area:** frontend-ui · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/components/panels/practice/PracticePanel.tsx:1063-1075` (`logs.map`, `Card
  key={log.fen}`, and the `Math.floor(node.halfMoves / 2) + 1` / `node.halfMoves % 2 === 0`
  formatting of `node.san`).
* **Defect:** two independent defects in the same four lines. (1) **Numbering is off by one side.**
  `log.fen` is the position the user was asked about, so `node` is that position and `node.san` is
  the move that *led into* it, whose ply is `halfMoves - 1`. Using the position's own parity
  renders the move played after `1.e4` as `1... e4` and the move after `1.e4 e5` as `2. e5`, where
  the correct renderings are `1. e4` and `1... e5`. (2) **`key={log.fen}` repeats.** Reviewing the
  same position twice — the normal case for spaced repetition — produces two log entries with the
  same FEN and therefore two React children with the same key.
* **Why it matters:** every line of the review history is labelled with the wrong move number, which
  is the one thing that makes a log entry identifiable; and the duplicate keys make React reuse or
  drop siblings, so entries can render with a neighbour's data after a re-render.
* **Candidate fix:** number from the move's own ply — `Math.floor((node.halfMoves - 1) / 2) + 1`
  with the inverted parity — or reuse the existing shared move-numbering helper rather than a third
  inline copy of the formula; and key the card by the log's position in the list combined with its
  review timestamp, or by the review id if one is introduced. `f-20260909-06` (handled) is the same
  class of numbering defect in a different place and records the custom-start-FEN case this formula
  also ignores.
* **Found by:** `review-chess-semantics` (blocker, confidence 95) in round 1 of the plan review for
  `f-20260906-23`, 2026-09-22; the duplicate-key half was found by the orchestrator while verifying
  it. Both verified in source. Filed rather than folded in: the plan for `f-20260906-23` changes how
  the modal *loads* its entries, not how it renders one, and no obligation of that mandate fails
  without this (rule 12a adoption gate).

## 2026-09-22 — filed through the inbox spool

### `parseLcov` coerces malformed counter lines instead of rejecting them

* **ID:** f-20260922-05 · **Status:** handled · **Area:** gate-scripts · **Root:** - · **Entry:** build · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `scripts/coverage-report.mjs`, `parseLcov` — the `DA`, `FN`, `FNDA` and `BRDA` branches and the `addCounter` helper they share.
* **Defect:** every counter value is passed through `Number(...)` and every identity is built by string concatenation, with no validation that either is well-formed. Measured 2026-09-22 on this parser: `DA:bogus,1` is accepted and counted as a **covered** line under the identity `bogus:`, inventing a covered record for a line number that does not exist; `DA:1,bogus` yields `Number("bogus")` → `NaN`, which `Math.max(0, NaN)` propagates as `NaN`, and `NaN > 0` is false, so the line is silently counted as uncovered instead of reported. A truncated or corrupt LCOV therefore produces a plausible report rather than a failure, and the gate can be **green on input it could not parse**.
* **Why it matters:** two coverage ratchets and both area-floor gates cite this script's exit status as evidence, in CI and on every local push, and the numbers they compare come entirely from this parser. A corrupt LCOV that yields *higher* covered counts passes the ratchet and then becomes the baseline the next run is measured against — the same shape as `f-20260920-18`, where a broken measurement was green in the direction that mattered. The blank-measurement guard added for `f-20260920-19` does not help: it fires on a record with no counters at all, not on one whose counters are nonsense.
* **Candidate fix:** decide, and then enforce, what this parser must reject — at minimum a non-integer line number, block or branch index, and a non-integer hit count where the format does not permit one. `BRDA` already has a legitimate non-numeric hit value (`-`, meaning "not taken"), so the rule is per field rather than blanket, and the answer has to be measured against **both** instruments this one script serves: `@vitest/coverage-v8` for the frontend and `llvm-cov` for the backend. That measurement is the work — a blanket "reject anything non-numeric" risks a false red on a valid variant one of the two emits, which is why this is filed rather than fixed inline.
* **Open question:** which counter fields must be rejected rather than coerced, and is rejection even the right answer for a *partially* corrupt LCOV? A parser that throws on the first malformed line turns a salvageable report into a red gate, while one that drops the offending record silently shrinks the denominator — which is the class `f-20260920-19` exists to stop. A third option is to count malformed lines and fail only above a threshold, which needs a threshold nobody has evidence for. The answer decides whether this is a guard inside `parseLcov`, a separate validation pass over the LCOV text before parsing, or a per-record diagnostic that the blank-measurement check consumes.
* **Known limit to pin either way:** whatever is decided, the failure matrix in `scripts/coverage-report.mjs`'s header must gain the rows, since it currently names this tolerance as the one thing it does not cover.
* **Found by:** `review-error-handling` (blocker, confidence 98) in the `$push` review of `f5d27fda..HEAD`, 2026-09-22, and reproduced by the orchestrator against the parser before filing. Deferred rather than fixed in that run because the repair is a design question about what an LCOV parser must reject, needing its own measurement against two instruments — not because of effort or scope. The run that found it hardened the same file and recorded the gap in the artefact's own header at the same time.

**A second shape of the same class, found in the `$push` review of `f5d27fda..HEAD`, 2026-09-22, and measured.** `review-correctness` (blocker, 96): an `FNDA` line with no matching `FN` in the same record creates a phantom function rather than being rejected, and the phantom makes two records for one file disagree with a single record carrying the union of their counters. Measured — `SF:a.ts` + `FN:1,f` in one record and `SF:a.ts` + `FNDA:1,f` in another merge to `{covered: 1, total: 2}`, while one record carrying both lines gives `{covered: 1, total: 1}`. The pairing of `FNDA` to `FN` is per record by construction, which is the LCOV convention, so this is malformed input reaching the same unvalidated path as the coerced counter values above rather than a separate defect.

It matters more since 2026-09-22 than before: `buildCoverageReport` now merges records for one file across `SF` spellings, so a malformed record no longer has to duplicate a whole file's spelling to interact with a well-formed one. Whatever this finding decides about rejecting malformed counters must decide this case with it — reject the record, drop the unmatched `FNDA`, or keep the phantom and say so — and the answer belongs in the same measurement against both instruments.
<!-- ledger-meta {"command":"annotate","effect_lines":4,"effect_sha256":"3dc97aa5d5175bd143d160e4ed0436e21e177c38991cffe1c0b55414861392f1","input_sha256":"dd4f18fcf19fc424d59c57332f870bbceff6ff9d951c341bfb555661be612941","kind":"mutation-receipt","operation":"d2860b30688598ae2dca1e240673244cc088b4c1fd2a54a471a9f40d595dd165","options":{"section":null},"request_id_sha256":null,"results":["f-20260922-05"],"target":"f-20260922-05","v":1} -->

* **Closed 2026-10-07** by drain session `3a3526b5-c266-4e01-a142-50f8bacec12e` (drain run `a28f99b3-2237-4fa8-b5ca-715d97e8cd6a`), adopting the reviewed plan `tasks/plans/2026-10-07-lcov-malformed-input-rejection.md` (plan review r1–r3, handoff `tasks/handoffs/2026-10-07-f-20260922-05-review.md`).
* **Decided:** reject, never coerce or salvage — `parseLcov` throws on the first violation (`d-20261007-28`); LCOV 2.x forms rejected (`d-20261007-29`); unknown keys stay ignored and summary lines are not cross-checked (`d-20261007-30`). The unmatched-`FNDA` phantom is rejected rather than kept or dropped. Rejected alternatives and reasons are in those entries.
* **Done:** every `DA`/`FN`/`FNDA`/`BRDA` field is checked against a per-key grammar measured on both instruments (canonical decimals, lines ≥ 1, `BRDA` taken `-` allowed, exact field counts), plus record structure (`SF`/`end_of_record` pairing, no counter outside a record, no open record at end of input) and `FNDA`→`FN` pairing, unconditionally before `includeLine` exclusion. The message names the input line, rule, raw line and open `SF`; the CLI exits 1 before any baseline write. Failure-matrix rows 93–113 (114 paths), each CLI-staged; real-instrument negative controls recorded in the header. Commits `7885ca19`, `f3aedb9f`, `0e5d2fc9`; decisions `09a75b7f`, `aeb1111d`, `db3b3de5`.
* **Proof:** `pnpm coverage:report:test` 258/258; `pnpm gate:ensure frontend-coverage` and `backend-coverage` green on freshly regenerated LCOV from `@vitest/coverage-v8` and `llvm-cov` with unchanged baselines and floors; four damaged copies of that output each exit 1 with the expected message.

### The migrated `deck-*` browser keys are left in place and need a later deletion pass

* **ID:** f-20260922-06 · **Status:** open · **Area:** frontend-state · **Root:** - · **Entry:** inline · **Blocked:** none
* **Where:** `src/state/practiceStorage.ts` (the startup migration pass planned by
  `tasks/plans/2026-09-22-practice-durable-storage.md`), `src/state/pathOwners.ts:177-191`,
  `src/routes/__root.tsx:143-152`.
* **Defect:** the practice-persistence change migrates every `deck-<id>-<game>` value into the
  native store and then **leaves the browser key in place**, marked migrated by the native envelope.
  The migrated copy therefore keeps occupying the ~5 MB localStorage quota it already occupied, and
  two copies of the same learning history exist until this is cleaned up.
* **Why it is deferred rather than done there:** `localStorage` has no compare-and-swap, so between
  the final `getItem` and the `removeItem` another writer can extend or replace the value and have
  that write deleted. The only writer that ever wrote these keys is a **pre-upgrade build of the
  application**, which can run concurrently — two instances share one webview data directory and
  `src-tauri/src/main.rs:2424-2437` installs no single-instance plugin. Five rounds of plan review
  were spent trying to make that deletion safe before the plan withdrew it; the honest answer is that
  it is safe only once no pre-upgrade build can plausibly still be in use.
* **Fix shape:** once that is true, delete the key after a successful migration, and drop the legacy
  half of the startup path-owner union in `pathOwners.ts` at the same time — it exists only because
  the keys are still there. Until then nothing should try to be cleverer about it.
* **Depends on:** `f-20260906-23` shipping first; this is the follow-up, not an alternative to it.
* **Found by:** the plan review for `f-20260906-23`, rounds 4 and 5, 2026-09-22 — `review-plan`
  (confidence 98), `review-correctness` (99), `review-root-cause`, `review-error-handling` and
  `review-code-quality` each produced the same loss sequence independently.
